title: Asking politely · hoping
titleJp: ゆっくり話していただけませんか
canDo: I can make the same request at 4 levels of politeness, from 〜てください to 〜ていただけませんか, and pick the level for the person I'm talking to.
I can ask a friend for a favor casually (〜てくれない？) and a colleague with 〜てくれませんか or 〜てもらえませんか.
I can ask a teacher or a stranger in Japan for help with 〜ていただけませんか: もう少しゆっくり話していただけませんか。
I can accept a request with いいですよ and decline it with すみません、ちょっと…
I can wish someone well with 〜といいですね and state a hope of my own, with some worry, with 〜といいんですが.

blocks.t: Warm-up: say the て-form of 開ける, 貸す, 待つ, 教える and 話す out loud, the potential of もらう (もらえる, lesson 13-1), and one favor you received with 〜てくれました (lesson 16-1)
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice
Grammar: the 3 points, each with its examples read aloud and one 🔬. In your notebook, draw the request ladder, one step per form
Block 6: the Lesson 16 video (only the part about 〜ていただけませんか and 〜といい) or the Sakubi sections, as a second explanation
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: 〜てくれる and 〜てもらう (lesson 16-1): the direction of the favor. The requests in this lesson are questions made with those same verbs.
The potential form (lesson 13-1): もらう → もらえる and いただく → いただける. Without it, the polite request doesn't work.
〜てください (lesson 06-2), the first step of the ladder, and declining politely with ちょっと… (lesson 03-3).
Present short forms, affirmative and negative, of verbs, adjectives and nouns (lesson 08-1): they are what comes before といい.
〜んです (lesson 12-1) and が meaning "but" (lesson 08-3), which together make 〜といいんですが.

vocab.en: to open (a window, a door: 〜を開ける)
to call (タクシーをよぶ = to call a taxi)
to go well, to work out
to be found, to turn up (something you were looking for: 〜が見つかる)
to be in time, to make it (〜に間に合う)
to get better; to be fixed (the pair of なおす, lesson 16-1)

grammar.title: The request ladder: 〜てくれませんか and 〜てもらえませんか
grammar.gloss: asking for a favor, from the most direct to the kindest
grammar.explanation:
You can already ask with **〜てください** (lesson 06-2). It is polite in form, but it is a **direct** request: it sounds like "please do it", almost an instruction. To ask for a **favor**, Japanese usually turns the request into a **negative question** made with the favor verbs from lesson 16-1. The more indirect the question, the more polite the request. Think of a ladder:
• **〜てください**: "please do…". The most direct step. Good for instructions and for people close to you.
• **〜てくれませんか**: "won't you … (for me)?". くれる already says the favor comes to me. Good with colleagues and acquaintances.
• **〜てもらえませんか**: "couldn't I receive from you the favor of …?". もらえる is the **potential** of もらう (lesson 13-1): you ask whether it is **possible** to receive the favor, and that makes the request a little softer.
• **〜ていただけませんか**: the top step, with いただく (point b).
• The difference between くれませんか and もらえませんか is small, and both work in most everyday situations.

English has a ladder too: "Open the window, please" → "Would you open the window?" → "Could you possibly open the window?" Japanese climbs it by changing the verb at the end.

**How to build it.** て-form + くれ / もらえ + ませんか. The whole request sits in the **PREDICATE**, at the end: 開けてくれませんか is one block. Read from it: "won't you open (for me)?" → what? → the window.
• The one who will do the favor is **the listener**, so they almost never appear in the sentence. You don't need 私に either: くれる and もらう already show that the favor is for you.
• The particles are still the verb's own: まどを開ける → まどを開けてくれませんか.
• The negative question (〜ませんか) usually sounds softer than the affirmative one (〜ますか), because it leaves room for the person to say no. Both exist. The negative is only politeness, as in English "Couldn't you…?": nobody hears a real "not" in it, so you answer the request itself (いいですよ, or すみません、ちょっと…).
• Among friends, the request drops ます and becomes casual: **〜てくれない？** or **〜てもらえない？** (also 〜てくれる？ / 〜てもらえる？), with your voice rising at the end.
grammar.structure: [object] を [て-form] くれませんか / もらえませんか。 · casual: [て-form] くれない？

examples.jp: ちょっとまどを開けてくれませんか。— いいですよ。
examples.kana: ちょっとまどをあけてくれませんか。— いいですよ。
examples.romaji: Chotto mado o akete kuremasen ka. — Ii desu yo.
examples.en: Could you open the window for a moment? — Sure.

examples.jp: すみません、写真をとってもらえませんか。
examples.kana: すみません、しゃしんをとってもらえませんか。
examples.romaji: Sumimasen, shashin o totte moraemasen ka.
examples.en: Excuse me, could you take a photo for me?

examples.jp: ねえ、あしたノートを貸してくれない？
examples.kana: ねえ、あしたノートをかしてくれない？
examples.romaji: Nē, ashita nōto o kashite kurenai?
examples.en: Hey, can you lend me your notebook tomorrow?

pitfalls: In a request for yourself, the verb is くれる, not あげる: ノートを貸してあげませんか ✗ (sounds like "how about lending it to someone?") → ノートを貸してくれませんか ✓.
With もらう, the request needs the potential: 写真をとってもらいませんか ✗ (sounds like a suggestion: "how about we get someone to take it?") → 写真をとってもらえませんか ✓.
In casual speech, the intonation is what makes it a question. 貸してくれない。 with a falling voice ✗ (it sounds like a complaint: "he won't lend it to me") → 貸してくれない？ with your voice rising at the end ✓.
howToStudy: Take one request, "lend me the pen" (ペンを貸す), and say the 4 steps out loud, from the most direct to the most polite: 貸してください → 貸してくれませんか → 貸してもらえませんか → 貸していただけませんか.

Tap 🔬 on example 1: ちょっと is HOW / HOW OFTEN, まどを is the OBJECT and 開けてくれませんか is the PREDICATE. Under the predicate, the 🔬 writes "invitation / suggestion", because the sentence ends in 〜ませんか, like the invitations of lesson 03-3. Here it is not an invitation: with くれる, it is a request for a favor for you.
Think of 3 people close to you (a friend, a colleague, a family member) and make a real request to each one out loud, casually (〜てくれない？) or with 〜てくれませんか.

grammar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
grammar.gloss: "could you possibly…?": the most polite request
grammar.explanation:
In lesson 16-1 you saw that **いただく** is the humble form of もらう. It builds the top step of the ladder: **て-form + いただけませんか**. いただける is the **potential** of いただく, just as もらえる is the potential of もらう. Literally: "couldn't I (humbly) receive the favor of …?".
• Use it with **teachers, bosses, customers and strangers**, especially when the favor takes some effort. It is the request you will use in Japan to ask for help on the street, in a shop or at a hotel.
• With a superior, 〜てください can sound like an instruction. 先生、見てください works in a classroom, but to ask your teacher for a favor, 見ていただけませんか sounds much kinder.
• It is common to open the request with **すみませんが、** ("sorry, but…") or with **ちょっと**, which soften it even more.
• Why the top step is the longest: in Japanese politeness, **longer and more indirect usually means more polite** — polite phrases work almost like euphemisms. 見てください (6 beats) → 見ていただけませんか (10 beats).
• The structure is the same as in point a: the whole request sits in the **PREDICATE**, at the end. The one who will do the favor is the listener. When their name appears, it comes first, followed by a comma, as CALLING: 先生、….

**How to answer.** To accept: **いいですよ** or **ええ、いいですよ**. In shops and hotels you will hear **かしこまりました** ("certainly, understood"). To decline without saying "no", Japanese usually uses すみません + ちょっと… and leaves the sentence hanging, as in lesson 03-3: すみません、あしたはちょっと…
• Going further (Sakubi): polite Japanese keeps **humble** words (you lower yourself: いただく, from もらう) apart from **respectful** ones (you raise the other person: くださる, from くれる). So 〜てくださいませんか is just as polite as 〜ていただけませんか. You will meet both families in Lessons 19 and 20.
grammar.structure: ([person]、) [object] を [て-form] いただけませんか。

examples.jp: 先生、もう少しゆっくり話していただけませんか。— ええ、いいですよ。
examples.kana: せんせい、もうすこしゆっくりはなしていただけませんか。— ええ、いいですよ。
examples.romaji: Sensei, mō sukoshi yukkuri hanashite itadakemasen ka. — Ē, ii desu yo.
examples.en: Professor, could you speak a little more slowly? — Yes, of course.

examples.jp: すみません、駅までの道を教えていただけませんか。
examples.kana: すみません、えきまでのみちをおしえていただけませんか。
examples.romaji: Sumimasen, eki made no michi o oshiete itadakemasen ka.
examples.en: Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?

examples.jp: 田中さん、あしたひっこしをてつだっていただけませんか。— すみません、あしたはちょっと…
examples.kana: たなかさん、あしたひっこしをてつだっていただけませんか。— すみません、あしたはちょっと…
examples.romaji: Tanaka-san, ashita hikkoshi o tetsudatte itadakemasen ka. — Sumimasen, ashita wa chotto...
examples.en: Mr./Ms. Tanaka, could you help me with the move tomorrow? — Sorry, tomorrow is a bit…

pitfalls: The request needs the potential: 教えていただきませんか ✗ → 教えていただけませんか ✓. Watch the け: いただ**け**ませんか.

〜ていただけませんか asks for a favor; it does not offer help. To offer, you still use 〜ましょうか (lesson 16-1): 先生、にもつを持っていただけませんか ✗ (if you meant "shall I carry it?": you just asked your teacher to carry it!) → 先生、にもつを持ちましょうか ✓.
With close friends this step sounds distant, as if you weren't friends: (to a friend) ノートを貸していただけませんか ✗ → ノートを貸してくれない？ ✓.
howToStudy: Say out loud 5 requests a foreigner uses in Japan, all with 〜ていただけませんか: もう一度言って / ゆっくり話して / 写真をとって / 道を教えて / ちょっと待って.

Tap 🔬 on example 3. In the question, 田中さん shows up as CALLING (the person you are talking to), あした is TIME, ひっこしを is the OBJECT and てつだっていただけませんか is the PREDICATE. In the answer, the 🔬 tags ちょっと as the PREDICATE, labeled "set phrase": it is the polite "no" from lesson 03-3.
Speaking: record yourself making the same request to two people, a friend (〜てくれない？) and a teacher (すみませんが、〜ていただけませんか). Listen and notice how the polite sentence is longer and calmer.

grammar.title: 〜といいですね / 〜といいんですが
grammar.explanation:
To say "I hope…", Japanese uses **short form + といい**. Literally it is "if [this happens], it will be good". This と is the "natural consequence" if: X と Y says that when X happens, Y follows (you will study it fully in lesson 18-3). So 〜といい = "if X happens, things will be good". The block ending in と is the **condition** (the 🔬 calls it IF / WHEN), and いい, at the end, is the **PREDICATE**.
• **〜といいですね**: a wish **for the other person**, about something they are going through, or for both of you. It is what you say when you are rooting for someone: めんせつ、うまくいくといいですね。
• **〜といいんですが**: a wish **of your own**, with a little worry or doubt. The が at the end is "but" (lesson 08-3), and the sentence is left hanging: "it would be good if…, but I'm not sure". The ん is the 〜んです of lesson 12-1. Among friends: **〜といいんだけど**.
• Talking to yourself or with friends, you will also hear **〜といいな** ("I hope…").

**What comes before と.** The **present** short form, affirmative or negative, even when you are talking about the future:
• Verb: うまくいく → うまくいくといい; ふらない → 雨がふらないといい.
• い-adjective, as is: やさしい → 試験がやさしいといい.
• な-adjectives and nouns need **だ**: 元気だといい, 休みだといい. In the negative: 雨じゃないといい.
• When the wish is about someone **being able** to do something, the potential (lesson 13-1) fits well: 英語が話せるといいんですが.

Don't confuse it with 〜たい (lesson 11-1): 〜たい is **your** wish to **do** something. 〜といい is hoping that a **situation** happens, and it works for you and for others. English "I hope" stays the same whoever the hope is for; Japanese picks the ending by whose hope it is.
grammar.structure: [present short form] といいですね。 · [present short form] といいんですが。 · [N / な-adj] だといい

examples.jp: あしたのめんせつ、うまくいくといいですね。
examples.kana: あしたのめんせつ、うまくいくといいですね。
examples.romaji: Ashita no mensetsu, umaku iku to ii desu ne.
examples.en: I hope your interview tomorrow goes well!

examples.jp: 日曜日のバーベキュー、雨がふらないといいですね。
examples.kana: にちようびのバーベキュー、あめがふらないといいですね。
examples.romaji: Nichiyōbi no bābekyū, ame ga furanai to ii desu ne.
examples.en: I hope it doesn't rain on Sunday's barbecue!

examples.jp: ホテルの人が英語を話せるといいんですが。
examples.kana: ホテルのひとがえいごをはなせるといいんですが。
examples.romaji: Hoteru no hito ga eigo o hanaseru to ii n desu ga.
examples.en: I hope the hotel staff can speak English… (I'm a little worried).

pitfalls: To root for someone, don't use たい: (to a sick friend) 早く元気になりたいですね ✗ → 早く元気になるといいですね ✓.
For something that hasn't happened yet, use the present before と: あした、雨がふらなかったといいですね ✗ → あした、雨がふらないといいですね ✓.
Nouns and な-adjectives need だ: 休みといいですね ✗ → 休みだといいですね ✓; 元気といいですね ✗ → 元気だといいですね ✓.
About a problem that is only yours, 〜といいですね sounds as if you were asking the other person to agree. For a wish of your own, with worry: 私の試験がやさしいといいですね ✗ → 試験がやさしいといいんですが ✓.
howToStudy: Think of 3 people who are going through something (an exam, a trip, an illness) and say a 〜といいですね out loud for each one. Then say 2 wishes of your own, with worry, with 〜といいんですが.

Tap 🔬 on example 3: ホテルの is DESCRIBES NEXT (人), 人が is the SUBJECT, 英語を is the OBJECT, 話せると is IF / WHEN and いいんですが is the PREDICATE, labeled "explanation (～んです)". Read from the end: "it would be good, but…" → if what? → if they can speak English → who? → the hotel staff. In examples 1 and 2 the 🔬 is switched off, because the engine can mistake the と of といいですね for a QUOTE (as with 言う). If you see that in your Journal, remember: here と means IF / WHEN.
Write 4 wishes in your notebook, each with a different kind of word before と: a verb, a negative verb, an い-adjective and a noun with だ.

media.title: Genki II · Lesson 16: the dialogue, vocabulary and grammar notes on 〜ていただけませんか and 〜といい
media.when: Before this lesson or right after the grammar block. The favors (〜てあげる／てくれる／てもらう) were in lesson 16-1; 〜時 and 〜てすみませんでした are in lesson 16-3.

media.title: Japanese Ammo with Misa: polite requests, from 〜てください to 〜ていただけませんか
media.where: YouTube · Japanese Ammo with Misa channel
media.search: Japanese Ammo with Misa polite requests ていただけませんか
media.when: After points a and b, to hear the request ladder explained another way

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Use kanji only for the ones you already know and write the rest in kana. Before each request, ask yourself: who am I talking to? That decides the step. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day. If you have the Genki II Workbook, do this lesson's exercises too; in this lesson, the ones on 〜ていただけませんか and 〜といい.

tasks.prompt: Take the request up to the top step: change 〜てください into 〜ていただけませんか.

items.q: もう一度言ってください。

a.jp: もう一度言っていただけませんか。
a.kana: もういちどいっていただけませんか。

items.note: Only the ending changes: ください → いただけませんか. The て-form (言って) stays the same.

items.q: ちょっと待ってください。

a.jp: ちょっと待っていただけませんか。
a.kana: ちょっとまっていただけませんか。

items.q: この漢字を読んでください。

a.jp: この漢字を読んでいただけませんか。
a.kana: このかんじをよんでいただけませんか。
a.romaji: Kono kanji o yonde itadakemasen ka.

items.q: 英語で説明してください。

a.jp: 英語で説明していただけませんか。
a.kana: えいごでせつめいしていただけませんか。
a.romaji: Eigo de setsumei shite itadakemasen ka.

items.note: The で ("in English") and the rest of the sentence don't change.

items.q: タクシーをよんでください。

a.jp: タクシーをよんでいただけませんか。

tasks.prompt: Pick the step for the person and write the whole request: friend → 〜てくれない？; colleague → 〜てくれませんか or 〜てもらえませんか; teacher, boss or stranger → 〜ていただけませんか.

items.q: (To a friend) Can you lend me your pen?

a.jp: ペンを貸してくれない？
a.kana: ペンをかしてくれない？

items.note: 〜てもらえない？ also works. Raise your voice at the end.

items.q: (To your teacher) Could you look at my composition?

a.jp: 作文を見ていただけませんか。
a.kana: さくぶんをみていただけませんか。

items.q: (To a colleague at work) Could you help me a little?

a.jp: ちょっとてつだってもらえませんか。

items.note: ちょっとてつだってくれませんか is also correct.

items.q: (To a stranger on the street) Could you take a photo of us?

a.jp: 写真をとっていただけませんか。
a.kana: しゃしんをとっていただけませんか。

items.note: With strangers, 〜てもらえませんか is also common. いただけませんか is the safest choice.

items.q: (To your boss) Could you lend me this book?

a.jp: この本を貸していただけませんか。
a.kana: このほんをかしていただけませんか。
a.romaji: Kono hon o kashite itadakemasen ka.

items.note: You are the one who gets the book, and いただく already says so. No need for 私に.

tasks.prompt: Hope for the situation: write the whole sentence with 〜といいですね (a wish for the other person, or for both of you) or 〜といいんですが (a wish of your own, with worry), using the words in parentheses.

items.q: Your friend has an exam tomorrow. (試験がやさしい)

a.jp: 試験がやさしいといいですね。
a.kana: しけんがやさしいといいですね。
a.romaji: Shiken ga yasashii to ii desu ne.

items.note: An い-adjective goes straight before と.

items.q: You have a cold and you are traveling on Saturday. (かぜが早くなおる)

a.jp: かぜが早くなおるといいんですが。
a.kana: かぜがはやくなおるといいんですが。
a.romaji: Kaze ga hayaku naoru to ii n desu ga.

items.note: It is your own problem, with worry: といいんですが.

items.q: Your friend is looking for an apartment. (いいアパートが見つかる)

a.jp: いいアパートが見つかるといいですね。
a.kana: いいアパートがみつかるといいですね。
a.romaji: Ii apāto ga mitsukaru to ii desu ne.

items.q: You are rushing to catch the train. (電車に間に合う)

a.jp: 電車に間に合うといいんですが。
a.kana: でんしゃにまにあうといいんですが。
a.romaji: Densha ni ma ni au to ii n desu ga.

items.q: Your colleague is about to meet the new boss. (やさしい人)

a.jp: やさしい人だといいですね。
a.kana: やさしいひとだといいですね。
a.romaji: Yasashii hito da to ii desu ne.

items.note: It ends in a noun (人), so だ goes before と.

items.q: You and a friend are going to the beach on Sunday. (天気がいい)

a.jp: 天気がいいといいですね。
a.kana: てんきがいいといいですね。
a.romaji: Tenki ga ii to ii desu ne.

items.note: It is a situation for both of you: といいですね. The two いい are normal: the first is the good weather; the second is the "I hope".

tasks.prompt: Write 4 sentences that are true or possible in your life: a request to a teacher with 〜ていただけませんか, a casual request to a friend, a wish for someone with 〜といいですね and a wish of your own, with worry, with 〜といいんですが. Then read them aloud and record yourself on your phone.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: 先生、この手紙の日本語をチェックしていただけませんか。ねえ、あしたかさを貸してくれない？マリアさん、あしたの試験、うまくいくといいですね。来週の旅行、雨がふらないといいんですが。
a.kana: せんせい、このてがみのにほんごをチェックしていただけませんか。ねえ、あしたかさをかしてくれない？マリアさん、あしたのしけん、うまくいくといいですね。らいしゅうのりょこう、あめがふらないといいんですが。
a.romaji: Sensei, kono tegami no nihongo o chekku shite itadakemasen ka. Nē, ashita kasa o kashite kurenai? Maria-san, ashita no shiken, umaku iku to ii desu ne. Raishū no ryokō, ame ga furanai to ii n desu ga.
a.en: Professor, could you check the Japanese in this letter? Hey, can you lend me an umbrella tomorrow? Maria, I hope your exam tomorrow goes well! I hope it doesn't rain on next week's trip…

items.note: Check: the け in いただけませんか, the casual request with your voice rising at the end (？), the present short form before と, だ after a noun or な-adjective, and といいですね for the other person × といいんですが for yourself.

practice.what: If you can, play in an N4 area of the game. Hunt for requests in the dialogues: 〜てください, 〜てくれませんか or 〜てくれない？, 〜てもらえませんか, 〜ていただけませんか. For each one, say out loud which step of the ladder it is on and who is asking whom. Also hunt for といい ("I hope"). Log the session in Immersion → Games, paste one of those lines into 🔬 Anatomy and save it with ⛏ Mining (fill in its new word with the 📖 Dictionary button).

Reviews first (🌊 All). Add the block 3 words that are missing from your deck with ⛏ Mining, as whole words so each kanji comes with its reading (試験, 見つかる, 間に合う…). Then, in the Journal, write 3 requests you would make in Japan (on the street, at a hotel, in a shop) with 〜ていただけませんか. Open "Anatomy of what I wrote" and check that the whole request ended up in the PREDICATE.

Resources tab → Tadoku's free graded readers (a level 2 or 3 story) or an easy manga you own. Hunt for requests (〜てくれない？, 〜てもらえませんか…) and hopes (〜といいな, 〜といいね). For each request, say who is asking whom and which step of the ladder it is on. Follow the story; don't look up every word.
Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times. いただけませんか has 8 equal beats (い・た・だ・け・ま・せ・ん・か): don't swallow the け.

Act out 3 travel scenes out loud: asking someone to take your photo, asking the way to the station and asking someone to speak more slowly. Record it in 40 seconds or less and check that every request came out with いただけませんか.

culture.title: "Reading the air": くうきを よむ
culture.body: 空気を読む, literally "to read the air", means sensing what the people around you think or want **without anyone spelling it out**, and acting on it. Often people in Japan prefer hinting to asking: in a cold room, someone may just say ちょっとさむいですね, hoping someone else will offer to close the window. That is why the requests in this lesson usually come as questions and with cushions like すみませんが and ちょっと: they leave room for the other person to say no without embarrassment. Someone who misses these cues is called 空気が読めない人, and the abbreviation **KY** (from *kūki ga yomenai*) even became slang. This doesn't mean nobody speaks directly: among friends, and with foreigners, many people are quite direct.
culture.try: Practice responding to the hint. When you hear ちょっとさむいですね, offer: まどをしめましょうか。 And to ask for help the Japanese way, start with the situation and leave the sentence hanging: すみません、道がわからないんですが… Often the other person will offer to help.

checklist: I can make the same request at all 4 steps without looking: 〜てください → 〜てくれませんか → 〜てもらえませんか → 〜ていただけませんか.
I know that もらえる and いただける are potentials, and I don't forget the け in いただけませんか.
I pick the step for the person: casual with friends (〜てくれない？, with my voice rising), いただけませんか with teachers, bosses and strangers.
I can accept a request with いいですよ and decline one with すみません、ちょっと…
I can wish someone well with 〜といいですね and state a hope of my own, with worry, with 〜といいんですが.
I put the present short form before と, with だ after nouns and な-adjectives.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
If I have the Genki II Workbook, I did the exercises on 〜ていただけませんか and 〜といい.
